  In code, two slots keep their older names: `dataset.col("date")` is the `time` slot and `dataset.col("label")` is the `target`.
</Callout>

## Draft and approved [#draft-and-approved]

A column map starts as a **draft**: the kit's proposal. A proposal can be wrong. In `amazon_sales`, `STATUS` gives the answer away; the kit warns about it and the model leaves it out.

Nothing downstream uses a draft. Explore, Ask and Share open only an **approved** dataset. A step given a draft raises `DescriptorNotApproved`, and the message says how to approve it.

## Who approves [#who-approves]

**You do.** Approval is the step where a person confirms the roles the kit proposed. A model never approves roles, and the kit never chooses the **target** for you.

<Tabs items="['Guided card', 'Code', 'Terminal']">
  <Tab value="Guided card">
    In the quickstart, on the column map card: look at **Check these first**, correct what is wrong, then press **Approve column map**.
  </Tab>

  <Tab value="Code">
    ```python
    role_review = nb.review_roles(connection, chosen_data)
    role_review.approve({"ZIP_CODE": "identifier"}, {"target": "CANCELLED"})   # the roles and slots you change
    dataset = role_review.dataset()
    ```

    Or, on a table directly:

    ```python
    draft = nb.describe("AMAZON.ORDER_LINES")
    draft.set(PRODUCT="category")
    draft.slot(target="CANCELLED")
    dataset = draft.approve()
    ```
  </Tab>

  <Tab value="Terminal">
    ```bash
    exakit describe AMAZON.ORDER_LINES --approve
    ```
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

## What approval checks and writes [#what-approval-checks-and-writes]

* Every column has a role, and no column sits in two slots.
* The table has not changed since it was profiled.
* The data is checked again, and a column that gives the target away is reported.
* The next **version** is written to the kit's store on this computer, under `~/.exasol-starter-kit/descriptors/`.
* The roles are published in Exasol Semantic Views: the schema's semantic model is rebuilt, with time, category and flag columns as dimensions and measures as facts and metrics. A sensitive column is never exposed. If publishing fails, the approval still stands and the message says why.
* The active workflow's log gets one line.

## Versions [#versions]

Every approval is a new version. Nothing is overwritten.

```python
nb.column_map_versions(dataset.id)     # every saved version, oldest first
nb.current_version(dataset.id)         # the approved one
```

Approving an older version's roles again brings it back as the newest version.

## Reference [#reference]

[`nb.describe`](/data-scientist/reference/describe#describe), [`nb.Draft`](/data-scientist/reference/describe#Draft), [`nb.review_roles`](/data-scientist/reference/role-picker#review_roles), [`nb.show_roles`](/data-scientist/reference/quickstart#show_roles), [`nb.column_map_versions`](/data-scientist/reference/descriptor-store#column_map_versions), [`nb.DescriptorNotApproved`](/data-scientist/reference/dataset#DescriptorNotApproved).


# Prepared views (/data-scientist/concepts/prepared-views)



Step 3, Prepare, looks at the data before anything is computed from it. It never changes your table. What it creates, when you ask, are views in the `EXAKIT_PREPARED` schema.

## Is the data clean? [#is-the-data-clean]

```python
findings = nb.data_checks(connection, dataset)
```

It looks for repeated keys, exact copies, gaps, placeholder values and a rare target. Each finding is one plain sentence that says what it does to a result. Deciding what to do about it is yours.

## Linked tables [#linked-tables]

```python
schema_map = nb.describe_schema(connection, dataset)
```

The schema map shows the tables that link to this one, with the evidence for each link. A link adds the other table's columns without adding rows.

To correct it: `schema_map.unlink("TABLE.COLUMN")` or `schema_map.link("TABLE.COLUMN", "TABLE.KEY")`.

The **joined view** combines the table with every linked table. It is a proposal until you create it:

```python
proposal = schema_map.joined_view(dataset)
joined = proposal.create(connection)       # only when you want it
```

## A typed, cleaned view [#a-typed-cleaned-view]

```python
proposal = nb.typed_view(connection, dataset)
prepared = proposal.create(connection)     # only when you want it
```

It proposes correct types for numbers and dates stored as text, turns blanks and placeholders into NULL, and removes exact copies. Read what changes before you create it.

In `01_explore`, `USE_JOINED = True` and `USE_PREPARED = True` in the first cell create these views and make the later steps read them.

## Columns that give the answer away [#columns-that-give-the-answer-away]

```python
leaking = nb.leakage_check(connection, dataset)
```

A column whose values almost decide the target on their own would make a model look better than it is. These columns are listed and left out of the model.

## Reference [#reference]

[Data checks](/data-scientist/reference/data-checks), [Schema map and joined view](/data-scientist/reference/schema-map), [Typed view](/data-scientist/reference/prepare).


# Sharing and hand-off (/data-scientist/concepts/sharing-and-handoff)



## A dashboard, preview first [#a-dashboard-preview-first]

Step 8 turns one checked result into a dashboard others open in a browser. Dashboards run on **Dash Server**, a kit add-on the notebook installs and starts for you.

1. `nb.share(...)` prepares a dashboard from approved roles and SQL you can read.
2. It goes up as a **preview**. You open it and check that the figures match the query.
3. Only then is it **published**: `dashboard_draft.confirm(dash_server, figures_checked=True)`.

A preview that was not checked is never promoted. In automated runs the check is never set, so nothing is published without a person.

## The hand-off bundle [#the-hand-off-bundle]

Step 9 packs the work into one folder and a zip.

```python
handoff = nb.handoff_bundle(connection, dataset)
```

It is written to `~/.exasol-starter-kit/bundles/<workflow id>/` and holds:

| File              | What it is                                                                                                            |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `descriptor.yaml` | The approved column map                                                                                               |
| `schema-map.json` | The schema map, when there is one                                                                                     |
| `queries.sql`     | Every query the workflow ran, with its digest and row count                                                           |
| `workflow.jsonl`  | The workflow log as it is                                                                                             |
| `README.md`       | What the data is, which column map version the numbers rest on, what was approved and published, and how to repeat it |

Nothing in it is a password.

## The training handoff [#the-training-handoff]

The ML Engineer's handoff is a different thing: one JSON file with the feature view, the target and a reproducible split, written by `nb.write_handoff(connection, dataset)` to `~/.exasol-starter-kit/handoffs/`. A stale one is refused, and `nb.handoff_is_stale` names what changed.

## Reference [#reference]

[Share a dashboard](/data-scientist/reference/share), [Dash Server tools](/data-scientist/reference/dash-mcp), [Hand-off bundle](/data-scientist/reference/handoff-bundle), [Training handoff](/data-scientist/reference/handoff).


# Sources (/data-scientist/concepts/sources)



Data reaches the notebooks in three ways. All three end the same way: a table or view the kit can describe, and a column map you approve.

## A kit dataset [#a-kit-dataset]

Practice data the kit offers. `tpch`, `energy` and `weather` come with the kit, and `amazon_sales` and `fraud_transactions` are downloaded when you load them. `nb.sample_datasets()` lists them and says which are loaded.

## Your own data [#your-own-data]

A CSV, Parquet, JSON or Excel file, a folder of them, or a table already in the database. Files are loaded with the kit's own loader, the one `exakit data-load` runs.

## An external source [#an-external-source]

A database or lake elsewhere: PostgreSQL, MySQL, Snowflake and others. The kit connects it as a **virtual schema**: its tables appear in your local Exasol as `VS_<NAME>` and are read from the source when you query them. Nothing is copied.

```python
nb.connectors()                      # every kind of source the kit can connect
nb.connector_inputs("postgresql")    # what that connector asks, required ones marked
nb.connected_sources(connection)     # the sources connected now
```

## A source with several kinds in one [#a-source-with-several-kinds-in-one]

A **Lakehouse** is one connector for several things: an Iceberg REST catalog, Unity Catalog, AWS Glue, or Parquet files in a plain folder, with the files on S3 or Azure. Two **settings** pick the combination, and each combination asks for different details.

In the **Data source** list it appears as a tree, the same one the terminal's connect menu shows:

```text
Lakehouse (Iceberg / Delta)
   Iceberg REST catalog
        Let the catalog give access
        Amazon S3 / S3-compatible
        Azure ADLS Gen2
   Unity Catalog
        ...
   AWS Glue
        Amazon S3 / S3-compatible
   No catalog - Parquet files in a folder
        Amazon S3 / S3-compatible
        Azure ADLS Gen2
```

* Pick a **leaf** and both settings are chosen.
* A setting the tree does not hold, such as the catalog login (token or OAuth), is asked in one more step.
* Pick **Lakehouse** itself and the settings are asked one by one.

In code the settings are plain inputs:

```python
form = nb.connector_inputs("lakehouse")
form["tree"]                                                        # the picks, as the tree shows them
form = nb.connector_inputs("lakehouse", catalog="unity", files="s3")
form["inputs"]                                                      # what that combination asks
nb.connect_source("lakehouse", "lake", catalog="unity", files="s3", workspace_url="https://...", namespace="main.sales")
```

Some combinations have **two secrets**: the catalog login and the storage keys. The login is asked like any password. The storage secret travels in a file only you can read, removed as soon as the kit has read it.

## One source engine [#one-source-engine]

The connectors, their inputs and the connection-string reader come from the kit's source engine, the one `exakit connect` runs. Nothing about a connector is defined in the notebooks, so a connector added to the kit appears in the form with no notebook change.

## Passwords [#passwords]

* A password is asked in a hidden box and handed to `exakit connect` on standard input.
* It is never written into a cell, the code view or the workflow log.
* A password inside a connection string is used and never shown.
* A second secret (a Lakehouse's storage keys) goes to the kit in a private file, never on a command line.

## Live sources and AI [#live-sources-and-ai]

A table from an external source is read from there as you query it. Before sampled rows from a live source go to a model, the notebook names the source and asks. Only a yes sends them.

## Reference [#reference]

[External sources](/data-scientist/reference/sources), [Your own file or table](/data-scientist/reference/own-file), [Data map](/data-scientist/reference/data-map).


# Workflow (/data-scientist/concepts/workflow)



A **workflow** gives one id to every query and decision in a piece of work. The quickstart starts it and the other notebooks continue it. You never paste an id.

```python
workflow_id = nb.workflow("data-scientist-quickstart")   # in the quickstart
nb.continue_workflow("explore")                          # in every later notebook
```

`continue_workflow` takes this kernel's workflow, else the last one started on this computer, and starts a new one only when there is none.

## What is logged [#what-is-logged]

While a workflow is active, every helper that does something appends one line to its log: a SQL statement, a column map draft or approval, a model trace, a dashboard revision, a hand-off. Every guided card action is a line too, with the code it ran and whether it worked.

Without a workflow nothing is written. There are no implicit workflows.

## Where the log is [#where-the-log-is]

`~/.exasol-starter-kit/workflows/<id>.jsonl`: one JSON object per line, append-only, readable by you only. The id looks like `wf-20261027-3f9a1c`.

```python
nb.list_workflows()              # every workflow on this computer
nb.workflow_log(workflow_id)     # one workflow's events
```

```bash
exakit workflow show wf-20261027-3f9a1c
```

## No secrets in the log [#no-secrets-in-the-log]

A secret-named value or a connection string with a password is refused before anything is written. SQL that looks credential-bearing, such as a statement with a PASSWORD or API_KEY column, is logged with its text replaced and its digest kept, and a warning is shown.

<Callout>
  A log that cannot be written warns and the cell goes on. Logging never fails the work it describes.
</Callout>

## Reference [#reference]

[Workflows](/data-scientist/reference/workflow).


# Review and approve the column map (/data-scientist/guides/approve-column-map)



This is step 2 of `00_quickstart`. Until the map is approved, Explore, Ask and Share have nothing to read. For what the roles and slots mean, see [Column map and approval](/data-scientist/concepts/descriptor).

<Steps>
  <Step>
    ### Open the review [#open-the-review]

    ```python
    role_review = nb.review_roles(connection, chosen_data)
    ```

    The kit profiles the table and proposes a role for every column.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Check the uncertain columns first [#check-the-uncertain-columns-first]

    **Check these first** lists the columns the kit was least sure about, each with the evidence that chose its role. Start there.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Correct roles and choose the target [#correct-roles-and-choose-the-target]

    Change a role where it is wrong. Choose the **target**: the outcome you want to predict. The kit never chooses it. Leave a slot empty when no column fits.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Approve [#approve]

    Press **Approve column map**, or in code:

    ```python
    role_review.approve({"ZIP_CODE": "identifier"}, {"target": "CANCELLED"})
    ```

    The first argument is the roles you change, the second the slots. With nothing to change, the saved approval stands.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Read it back [#read-it-back]

    ```python
    dataset = role_review.dataset()
    nb.show_roles(dataset)
    ```
  </Step>
</Steps>

## What you get at the end [#what-you-get-at-the-end]

An approved column map. It is saved as a new version, and the schema's [semantic model](/data-scientist/guides/semantic-views) in Exasol Semantic Views is rebuilt with it, so AI clients read the same meaning. Explore, Ask and Share read only an approved map.

## After approving [#after-approving]

```python
leaking = nb.leakage_check(connection, dataset)       # columns that give the outcome away
versions = nb.column_map_versions(dataset.id)         # every saved version
nb.data_map(connection)                               # all your data in one map
```

<Callout>
  Approval checks the data again. A warning about a column that gives the target away is not an error: the column stays in the map and is left out of the model.
</Callout>

## Change your mind later [#change-your-mind-later]

Open the quickstart, change the roles and approve again. That writes a new version. The other notebooks follow the newest approval when you run their first cell again.


# Ask your data (/data-scientist/guides/ask)



This is step 7, in `02_ask_your_data`.

<Steps>
  <Step>
    ### Ask [#ask]

    ```python
    QUESTION = "How many rows are in each category?"
    dataset = nb.dataset(connection, nb.chosen_dataset(None))
    nb.example_questions(dataset)      # questions this column map can answer
    ```
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Get a proposal [#get-a-proposal]

    Three ways to draft the SQL:

    ```python
    proposal = nb.draft_question(connection, dataset, QUESTION)     # the kit's rules: no model, nothing leaves this computer
    proposal = nb.ask(dataset, QUESTION)                            # your model drafts it from the column map
    proposal = nb.ask(dataset, QUESTION, proposed_sql="SELECT ...") # your own SQL
    ```

    With a model, only the approved column map and the question are sent. No rows.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Read it, and edit if needed [#read-it-and-edit-if-needed]

    A proposed query can be wrong: a wrong column, a missing filter. Read it.

    ```python
    proposal.edit("SELECT ...")        # replaces the SQL and removes any approval
    ```
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Approve and run [#approve-and-run]

    ```python
    proposal.approve()
    answer = proposal.run()
    ```

    Only the exact approved text runs, through the kit's read-only service as the read-only user. `answer` holds its result. Check the figures against the SQL.
  </Step>
</Steps>

<Callout type="warn">
  Nothing runs before `approve()`. In the notebook, set `APPROVE_SQL = True` and run the cell again.
</Callout>

See [AI and tracing](/data-scientist/concepts/ai-and-tracing) and [Set up a model](/data-scientist/guides/set-up-a-model).


# Explore and model (/data-scientist/guides/explore-and-model)



`01_explore` reads the dataset you approved. Its first cell holds the choices:

```python
DATASET = None          # None: the dataset approved last in the quickstart
USE_AI_THEMES = False   # True: your model sorts the texts into themes
USE_JOINED = False      # True: create and use the joined view
USE_PREPARED = False    # True: create and use the typed, cleaned view
```

## Prepare [#prepare]

```python
workflow_id = nb.continue_workflow("explore")
connection = nb.connect()
dataset = nb.review_roles(connection, nb.chosen_dataset(DATASET)).dataset(draft_ok=True)

findings = nb.data_checks(connection, dataset)
schema_map = nb.describe_schema(connection, dataset)
typed_view_proposal = nb.typed_view(connection, dataset)
```

Read the findings and the two proposals. Nothing is created until you set `USE_JOINED` or `USE_PREPARED`. See [Prepared views](/data-scientist/concepts/prepared-views).

## Explore [#explore]

Each query shows its SQL before its result, and a plain-language note under it.

```python
rows = nb.sql(connection, f"""
SELECT {dataset.col("category")} AS GROUP_, COUNT(*) AS N
FROM {dataset.fact_table}
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY N DESC""")
nb.show_sql()
```

`nb.note_groups` and `nb.note_trend` write the notes under the group and over-time results.

## Model and validate [#model-and-validate]

```python
leaking = nb.leakage_check(connection, dataset)
```

The notebook then reads up to 20,000 rows, trains a small baseline model on the category, the entity and the month, scores it on rows it has not seen, and shows what it leans on. `nb.note_model` says in plain words what the score means.

For more control, the **model lab** lets you choose the task, the model and the split:

```python
lab = nb.model_lab(connection, dataset)        # task, model and split are arguments
ideas = nb.feature_ideas(lab)                  # ideas, each with the SQL that would make it
result = nb.try_feature(lab, ideas[0])         # retrain with one idea added, on the same split
```

See [Model lab](/data-scientist/reference/lab).

<Callout>
  A dataset with no target skips the model steps and says so. Choose a target in the column map to run them.
</Callout>

## What you get at the end [#what-you-get-at-the-end]

The data checks, the schema map and the typed view proposal, the group and over-time results with their SQL, a small model with its score, and a note on what the score means.


# Load data (/data-scientist/guides/load-data)



All of this happens in step 1 of `00_quickstart`. On the **Choose your data** card you pick one of three boxes. The code below is what each box runs.

```python
import exakit.nb as nb

connection = nb.connect()
nb.check_connection(connection)
```

<Tabs items="['A kit dataset', 'Your own data', 'An external source']">
  <Tab value="A kit dataset">
    ```python
    nb.sample_datasets()                                   # what the kit has, and which are loaded
    sample_data = nb.load_sample(connection, "amazon_sales")
    ```

    A dataset that is not loaded yet is loaded first. Nothing else is needed.
  </Tab>

  <Tab value="Your own data">
    A file or a folder:

    ```python
    own_data = nb.load_own_file("~/sales-data/orders.csv", "SALES", conn=connection)
    ```

    CSV, Parquet, JSON and Excel work. Leave the schema empty and it is named after the folder: `~/sales-data` becomes `SALES_DATA`.

    A table that is already in the database:

    ```python
    own_data = nb.use_table(connection, "MY_DATA.ORDERS")
    ```

    `nb.data_map(connection)` lists the tables in the database. The kit's own schemas are left out unless you pass `include_kit=True`.
  </Tab>

  <Tab value="An external source">
    The card walks through it one step at a time: an existing connection or a new one, the kind of source, a connection string or manual details, a name, the password, and optional settings.

    ```python
    nb.connectors()                                         # every kind of source
    reading = nb.read_connection_string("postgresql", "postgres://reader@192.168.64.1:5432/shop")
    reading["missing"]                                      # what the string did not give

    test = nb.test_source("postgresql", "sales", url="postgres://reader@192.168.64.1:5432/shop")
    connected = nb.connect_source("postgresql", "sales", url="postgres://reader@192.168.64.1:5432/shop")
    source_data = nb.load_source(connection, "VS_SALES.ORDERS")
    ```

    A source with several kinds in one, such as a Lakehouse, shows its choices as a tree under it in the **Data source** list. Pick the catalog and where its files are; the steps after it ask only what that combination needs. See [Sources](/data-scientist/concepts/sources).

    * **Test connection** checks the inputs and reaches the source from this computer. It changes nothing.
    * **Connect and use this data** runs `exakit connect`. The tables then appear as `VS_SALES`.
    * The password is asked in a hidden box. It is never part of the code.
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

## Use what you chose [#use-what-you-chose]

```python
chosen_data = nb.first(source_data, own_data, sample_data)   # the first one that is set
```

## What you get at the end [#what-you-get-at-the-end]

`chosen_data` is the table you picked, ready for the column map step.

Next: [approve the column map](/data-scientist/guides/approve-column-map).

<Callout type="warn">
  A source on this computer is not `localhost` from the database's point of view. On macOS use `192.168.64.1`. For a cloud source, allow this computer's public IP there; the card shows it.
</Callout>


# Run the kit from a notebook (/data-scientist/guides/run-the-kit)



Step 0 of the quickstart is the kit itself. Every command here is the same `exakit` a terminal runs, with its output streaming into the cell.

## See what is there [#see-what-is-there]

```python
kit_state = nb.kit_check()      # what is installed and running; changes nothing
nb.components()                 # the kit's parts, their versions and pending updates
nb.addons()                     # the marketplace's add-ons and their state
nb.sample_datasets()            # the kit's datasets, and which are loaded
nb.loaded_files()               # the files you loaded
nb.notebooks("data-scientist")  # this persona's notebooks, in order
```

## Change it [#change-it]

```python
nb.exakit("start")                                  # start the database
nb.addon_ready("dash-server")                       # install and start an add-on
nb.exakit("data-load", "fraud_transactions")        # load a kit dataset, a file or a folder
nb.exakit("logs", "dash-server")                    # a service's log
nb.kit_update()                                     # bring the kit and its add-ons up to date
```

`nb.exakit(...)` returns the run with its exit code, so a cell can act on it.

<Callout>
  A command run from a cell has no terminal, so a question it would ask takes its default. Give a choice up front instead: `nb.exakit("mcp-setup", env={"EXAKIT_MCP_CLIENTS": "claude"})`.
</Callout>

## Reference [#reference]

[Kit commands](/data-scientist/reference/kit-commands), [Kit facts](/data-scientist/reference/kit-facts).


# Build semantic views (/data-scientist/guides/semantic-views)



Approving a column map already published it in **Exasol Semantic Views**: the schema's model, with the table as an entity, its time, category and flag columns as dimensions and its measures as `total_` and `average_` metrics. This step builds one model across sources, so a question that needs orders **and** deliveries **and** targets is answered from one place.

## Before you start [#before-you-start]

* Every table you want in the model has an approved column map ([Approve the column map](/data-scientist/guides/approve-column-map)).
* An AI model is set up if you want it to propose the fields ([Set up a model](/data-scientist/guides/set-up-a-model)). Without one, the fields keep the names the column maps give.

## In the guided view [#in-the-guided-view]

1. Open **Understand** and scroll to **Semantic views**.
2. Tick the tables. They are listed with their origin: sample data, your data, external source. Pick as many as the question needs.
3. Give the model a name, for example `sales_360`.
4. Add the links across schemas, one per line: `SCHEMA.TABLE.COLUMN=SCHEMA.TABLE.KEY`. The approved links inside each schema are used by themselves.
5. Tick **Let the AI propose business names, synonyms and metrics**.
6. Click **Preview**. Read the dimensions and metrics of each view, what the AI proposed, and what was refused and why. Nothing is written yet.
7. Click **Publish the model**.

**Models in the database** lists every model. **Refresh it** rebuilds a model the kit built from the column maps and links approved since.

## In the notebook [#in-the-notebook]

The cell after the data map:

```python
SEMANTIC_NAME = "sales_360"
SEMANTIC_TABLES = ["AMAZON.ORDER_LINES", "MY_DATA.TARGETS", "VS_LOGISTICS.COURIER_DAILY"]
SEMANTIC_LINKS = ["AMAZON.ORDER_LINES.SHIP_STATE=VS_LOGISTICS.STATE_LOGISTICS.STATE"]
PUBLISH_SEMANTIC = False                 # True to publish
semantic = nb.semantic_model(connection, SEMANTIC_NAME, tables=SEMANTIC_TABLES, links=SEMANTIC_LINKS, ai=None,
                             preview=not PUBLISH_SEMANTIC)
semantic
```

`ai=None` asks the AI only when a model is set up. Run the cell, read the preview, then set `PUBLISH_SEMANTIC = True` and run it again. Semantic Views is installed the first time it is needed.

## What the AI is sent [#what-the-ai-is-sent]

Names, types, grains, column notes and a category's most frequent values. Never a row, never a sensitive column. Every metric it proposes is checked before it is used, and Semantic Views validates it again: a refused one is skipped and named.

## Ask the model [#ask-the-model]

```python
nb.semantic_sql(connection, """
SELECT ship_state, total_amount, orders_count
FROM SEM_SALES_360.ORDER_LINES
GROUP BY ship_state
""")
```

Your AI clients ask the same model through the Exasol MCP server.

## Keep it current [#keep-it-current]

Approving a column map rebuilds every model its table is in. After a new link or table:

```python
nb.refresh_semantic(connection, "sales_360")
```

## What you get at the end [#what-you-get-at-the-end]

A published semantic model, `SEM_<NAME>`, that notebooks and AI clients answer from by its business names. Its definition is kept in `~/.exasol-starter-kit/semantic/<name>.json`, so a refresh rebuilds it the same way.

For the commands behind it, see [Semantic views](/kit/data/semantic-views).


# Set up a model (/data-scientist/guides/set-up-a-model)



A model is optional. It is used to draft SQL in Ask and to sort texts into themes in Explore. The kit calls an endpoint that speaks the Chat Completions API: an external provider or a model on your own machine.

## The quickest way [#the-quickest-way]

```python
nb.model_setup()
```

It asks for anything missing, with the keys in a hidden box, says what is set, and prints the lines that set the same thing for every notebook.

## In a cell [#in-a-cell]

```python
nb.use_model("your-model-id", "https://your-provider/v1/")                     # this kernel only
nb.use_model("your-model-id", "https://your-provider/v1/", remember=True)      # every notebook of this kit
nb.use_model(langfuse_base_url="https://cloud.langfuse.com", remember=True)    # tracing
```

The API key is asked in a hidden box. With `remember=True` it is kept in the kit's credentials, readable by you only.

## Check and forget [#check-and-forget]

```python
nb.model_settings()                            # what is set, without secrets
nb.tracing()                                   # is Langfuse tracing on?
nb.forget_model(model=True, langfuse=True)     # delete what was remembered
```

## The settings behind it [#the-settings-behind-it]

| Setting                                                           | What it is                                                                    |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `EXAKIT_MODEL_ID`                                                 | The model's id                                                                |
| `EXAKIT_PROVIDER_BASE_URL`                                        | The endpoint's address                                                        |
| `EXAKIT_PROVIDER_API_KEY`                                         | The key                                                                       |
| `LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY`, `LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY`, `LANGFUSE_BASE_URL` | Turn tracing on                                                               |
| `EXAKIT_PROVIDER_HEADERS`, `EXAKIT_MODEL_TEMPERATURE`             | Optional. Sent only when set. Claude Opus 4.7 and later refuse a temperature. |

The model's id and address can also live in `~/.exasol-starter-kit/exakit.env`. Provider recipes are in `MODEL-PROVIDERS.md`, copied beside the notebooks.

## What you get at the end [#what-you-get-at-the-end]

`nb.model_settings()` shows what is set. The AI steps still wait for you to turn them on: `DRAFT_WITH_MODEL = True` in Ask, or `USE_AI_THEMES = True` in Explore.

<Callout type="warn">
  Never type a key into a cell. Use the hidden box, so the key is not saved in the notebook file.
</Callout>


# Share a dashboard and hand off (/data-scientist/guides/share)



<Steps>
  <Step>
    ### Prepare the dashboard [#prepare-the-dashboard]

    ```python
    dashboard_query = "SELECT ..."   # the query the dashboard shows: one you have read and checked
    dataset = nb.dataset(connection, nb.chosen_dataset(None))
    dashboard_draft = nb.share(dataset, dashboard_query, "Orders by category", "orders-by-category", measure="count")
    ```

    The dashboard is built from approved roles and a query you can read.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Start Dash Server [#start-dash-server]

    ```python
    nb.addon_ready("dash-server")
    ```

    It installs Dash Server when it is missing and starts it when it is stopped. This is what `exakit marketplace dash-server` and `exakit start dash-server` do. You can skip this step: the preview sets the server up by itself, on the card and in `nb.dash_tools()`.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Preview [#preview]

    ```python
    dash_server = nb.dash_tools()
    preview_path = dashboard_draft.preview(dash_server)
    print("Preview:", dash_server.url + preview_path)
    ```

    Open it. Check that the categories and counts match your SQL, and that the filters update both charts and the table.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Publish [#publish]

    ```python
    live_path = dashboard_draft.confirm(dash_server, figures_checked=True)
    ```

    Set `figures_checked=True` only when the preview matches the query. Keep the live address with your workflow id.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Hand off [#hand-off]

    ```python
    handoff = nb.handoff_bundle(connection, dataset)
    ```

    One folder and a zip under `~/.exasol-starter-kit/bundles/`. It needs no Dash Server and holds no password. See [Sharing and hand-off](/data-scientist/concepts/sharing-and-handoff).
  </Step>
</Steps>


# Guided and Code (/data-scientist/start/guided-and-code)



## The guided view [#the-guided-view]

Each Data Scientist notebook opens with cards that do the page's steps with buttons and forms.

| Notebook           | Its cards open with |
| ------------------ | ------------------- |
| `00_quickstart`    | `guide.start()`     |
| `01_explore`       | `guide.explore()`   |
| `02_ask_your_data` | `guide.ask()`       |
| `03_share`         | `guide.share()`     |

## The Docs button [#the-docs-button]

The first card of every notebook has a **Docs** button beside the logo. It opens this documentation in a new tab, on the guide for that notebook: loading data from the quickstart, exploring from `01_explore`, asking from `02_ask_your_data`, sharing from `03_share`.

## The Code switch [#the-code-switch]

Every card has a **Guided / Code** switch at its top right.

* **Code** turns that card, in place, into its code as cells: what it ran this session, in order, and the exact call behind each control. Each cell can be edited and run right there with **Run** or Shift+Enter, and shows what it printed or returned under it, like a notebook cell. It runs in the notebook's own session, so it sees the same connection and data as the cards. **Copy as cell** copies it into a cell of your own, and **Reset** puts the original back.
* **Guided** turns it back. Only that card changes. The connection, the chosen data and the approvals stay as they are.

The notebook's own cells sit under **The code behind this page**. In the kit's JupyterLab they are hidden until you choose **Show all the notebook's code cells** at the foot of a card's Code view. In Marimo the cards show stacked, and the cells open with their code visible.

## One call, two ways [#one-call-two-ways]

Every button, form and choice on a card is one `exakit.nb` call, and the same call is a cell in the notebook's code section. Clicking **Approve** and running `role_review.approve(...)` do the same thing.

<Callout>
  What a card shows is read from the kit when it draws: the datasets, connectors, add-ons and notebooks are not written into the card. A connector added to the kit appears in the form with no notebook change.
</Callout>

## The Home card [#the-home-card]

The first card of the quickstart is the kit itself. It has two tabs.

* **Your kit:** what is installed and running, the loaded datasets, your approved column maps and your workflows.
* **Marketplace:** every add-on with **Install**, **Start** and **Update** buttons. They run `nb.addon_ready(id)` and `nb.kit_update(id)`, which is what `exakit marketplace` and `exakit update` do in a terminal.

## One workflow per start [#one-workflow-per-start]

`guide.start()` starts a workflow. Every card action after it is one line in that workflow's log: the card, the action, the code it ran and whether it worked. See [Workflows](/data-scientist/concepts/workflow).


# The notebooks and the nine steps (/data-scientist/start/notebooks)



## Open the notebooks [#open-the-notebooks]

```bash
exakit notebook            # JupyterLab
exakit notebook marimo     # Marimo
```

Both open in your browser on the kit's own Python, with the kernel **Exasol (Starter Kit)**. That kernel knows where the kit's connection is, so no notebook asks for a host, a user or a password.

Your copies are in `~/.exasol-starter-kit/notebooks/starter-kit-notebooks/data-scientist/`. A notebook you edited is never overwritten by an update.

## The path [#the-path]

Run the notebooks in order. Each one continues the workflow the first one started, so you paste no id and copy nothing between them.

| Notebook           | Steps                                     | What you have at the end                                                    |
| ------------------ | ----------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `00_quickstart`    | 0 Check the kit, 1 Access, 2 Understand   | A connection, a loaded dataset and an approved column map                   |
| `01_explore`       | 3 Prepare, 4 Explore, 5 Model, 6 Validate | Clean data, comparisons by group and over time, a small model and its score |
| `02_ask_your_data` | 7 Ask with AI                             | An answer from SQL you read and approved                                    |
| `03_share`         | 8 Share, 9 Hand off                       | A published dashboard and one folder a colleague can repeat the work from   |

## The nine steps [#the-nine-steps]

<Steps>
  <Step>
    ### Access [#access]

    Connect, start a workflow and load data: a kit dataset, your own file, or an external source. See [Load data](/data-scientist/guides/load-data).
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Understand [#understand]

    Approve the column map: which column is the key, the time, the text, the target (the outcome to predict), the category and the entity. See [Column map and approval](/data-scientist/concepts/descriptor).
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Prepare [#prepare]

    Check the data is clean, see the tables linked to it, and optionally create a typed, cleaned view. See [Prepared views](/data-scientist/concepts/prepared-views).
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Explore [#explore]

    Compare groups and look at the data over time. Each query shows its SQL before its result.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Model [#model]

    Set aside columns that give the answer away, then train a small baseline model.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Validate [#validate]

    Score the model on rows it has not seen and see what it leans on.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Ask with AI [#ask-with-ai]

    Ask in plain language, read the proposed SQL, approve it, run it read-only. See [Ask your data](/data-scientist/guides/ask).
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Share [#share]

    Turn one checked result into a dashboard: a preview first, published after you check the figures. See [Share a dashboard](/data-scientist/guides/share).
  </Step>

  <Step>
    ### Hand off [#hand-off]

    Pack the column map, every query, the dashboards and the workflow log into one folder and a zip.
  </Step>
</Steps>

Step 0, at the top of the quickstart, checks the kit itself from the notebook. See [Run the kit from a notebook](/data-scientist/guides/run-the-kit).

## Rules every notebook follows [#rules-every-notebook-follows]

* **One assignment picks the data.** `SAMPLE = "..."` in the quickstart, `DATASET = "..."` in the others. `None` means the dataset approved last.
* **No column name is typed.** Queries are built from the approved roles, so the same notebook runs on any table.
* **AI is opt-in.** The AI steps stay off until you turn them on, and a model never approves roles.
* **A step that cannot run says why.** A dataset with no text column skips the text steps and tells you.


# Column maps (/kit/data/column-maps)



A **column map** (the descriptor) gives every column of a table a role. Notebooks and AI clients read it, so they all work from the same meaning. For the idea behind it, see [Column map and approval](/data-scientist/concepts/descriptor).

## Draft [#draft]

```bash
exakit describe AMAZON.ORDER_LINES
```

The table is profiled with SELECTs only. Nothing is written to the database. Every column gets one of eight roles, with its confidence and the evidence that chose it:

`key`, `time`, `measure`, `category`, `flag`, `text`, `identifier`, `other`.

* The draft is deterministic: the same table gives the same draft.
* A column whose values look like e-mail addresses, phone numbers, IBANs or postcodes is marked **sensitive**.
* The **target** is never drafted. Only a person sets it.

## Approve [#approve]

```bash
exakit describe AMAZON.ORDER_LINES --approve --role target=CANCELLED --owner dana
```

`--role <slot>=<COLUMN>` corrects a slot: `key`, `time`, `text`, `target`, `category`, `entity`. `<slot>=-` leaves it empty.

Approval:

* checks that every column has a role, that none sits in two slots, and that the table has not changed since it was profiled
* writes a new version, never rewriting an old one
* publishes the roles in [Exasol Semantic Views](/kit/data/semantic-views): the schema's semantic model is rebuilt with this table as an entity, readable by the read-only AI user. Semantic Views is installed first when the database does not have it yet.

Your own table is never commented. If publishing fails, the approval still stands and the message says why.

## What you get at the end [#what-you-get-at-the-end]

A new version of the column map, kept under `~/.exasol-starter-kit/descriptors/`, and the schema's semantic model (its views in `SEM_<SCHEMA>`) rebuilt from it. The notebooks and AI clients read the approved version from then on.

## See and compare [#see-and-compare]

```bash
exakit describe amazon_sales --show              # the current version
exakit describe amazon_sales --show --version 1  # an earlier one
exakit describe amazon_sales --versions          # every version
exakit describe orders --comments                # rebuild the schema's semantic model again
```

Add `--json` to any of them for a script.

## A whole schema [#a-whole-schema]

```bash
exakit describe --schema TPCH
```

This lists every table with its rows and key, and every many-to-one link between tables with its evidence. A link is a foreign key the database declares, or a column whose values are in another table's key (at most 0.1% of them may be missing). A name alone never makes a link.

```bash
exakit describe --schema TPCH --approve --unlink ORDERS.O_CLERK
```

`--link TABLE.COLUMN=TABLE.KEY` adds a link and `--unlink TABLE.COLUMN` removes one. The approved links become relationships of the schema's semantic model. To join tables of different schemas, build a [multi-source model](/kit/data/semantic-views).

## Where they are kept [#where-they-are-kept]

`~/.exasol-starter-kit/descriptors/<SCHEMA>.<TABLE>/`: the draft, every approved version and the current one.

## When the table changes [#when-the-table-changes]

Columns whose name and type did not change keep their approved roles. The rest are flagged, and you approve again.

## With an AI model [#with-an-ai-model]

When a model is set up, one call adds a one-line note per column. It is sent each column's name, type, role, evidence and top values, never a row and never a sensitive column. A note never decides a role.

## From a notebook [#from-a-notebook]

```python
draft = nb.describe("AMAZON.ORDER_LINES")
draft.slot(target="CANCELLED")
dataset = draft.approve()
```

See [Review and approve the column map](/data-scientist/guides/approve-column-map).


# Datasets (/kit/data/datasets)



The kit carries sample datasets to practise on. `exakit data-load` lists them and loads the ones you pick.

| Dataset              | Loaded by                   | Where it comes from                          |
| -------------------- | --------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| `tpch`               | General                     | Bundled with the kit, loads without internet |
| `energy`             | General                     | Bundled with the kit, loads without internet |
| `weather`            | General                     | Bundled with the kit, loads without internet |
| `amazon_sales`       | Data Scientist, ML Engineer | Downloaded when you load it                  |
| `fraud_transactions` | Data Scientist, ML Engineer | Downloaded when you load it                  |

## Downloaded datasets [#downloaded-datasets]

`amazon_sales` and `fraud_transactions` are archives in the kit's datasets release. An archive is fetched only when you load that dataset. The kit checks the archive's SHA-256 and every file's digest, and refuses a mismatch.

```bash
exakit data-load amazon_sales
```

## A dataset with a column map [#a-dataset-with-a-column-map]

`amazon_sales` and `fraud_transactions` each ship with an approved [column map](/kit/data/column-maps), so the notebooks can use them straight away. You can approve your own version at any time.

The ML Engineer persona is not offered in this release, so for now only Data Scientist and General load these datasets.

## Load one again [#load-one-again]

```bash
exakit data-load --force amazon_sales
```

<Callout type="warn">
  `--force` drops that dataset's tables and rebuilds them. Anything you changed in its schema is lost.
</Callout>

## Add a dataset to the kit [#add-a-dataset-to-the-kit]

A dataset is one folder in `data/datasets/`. Nothing else names it, so a new folder appears in the menu.


# Load data (/kit/data/load-data)



```bash
exakit data-load
```

On a terminal this opens a menu: the kit's datasets, your own data, or an external source. Name what you want to skip the menu.

<Tabs items="['A kit dataset', 'One file', 'A folder']">
  <Tab value="A kit dataset">
    ```bash
    exakit data-load amazon_sales
    ```

    See [Datasets](/kit/data/datasets) for the list.
  </Tab>

  <Tab value="One file">
    ```bash
    exakit data-load ./sales.csv
    ```

    It asks two things, whatever the file's kind: the file, then `SCHEMA.TABLE`. To answer up front:

    ```bash
    EXAKIT_DATA_FILE=./sales.json EXAKIT_DATA_TABLE=STARTER_KIT.SALES exakit data-load
    ```

    CSV, Parquet and JSON are loaded. JSON is split into tables by an engine the kit installs for you on macOS, Linux and WSL. A `;`-separated CSV is loaded with its delimiter. A tabular `.txt` or `.tsv` file is listed with the rename to `.csv` that the loader needs.
  </Tab>

  <Tab value="A folder">
    ```bash
    exakit data-load ~/exports
    ```

    Every CSV, Parquet and JSON (.json, .geojson) file at the folder's top level becomes one table named after the file. The schema is asked once:

    ```bash
    EXAKIT_DATA_FILE=~/exports EXAKIT_SCHEMA=SALES exakit data-load
    ```

    Subfolders are not scanned. Files of other kinds are ignored. Duplicates are skipped with the reason. On Windows, a folder's JSON files are listed as skipped.
  </Tab>
</Tabs>

## Running it again is safe [#running-it-again-is-safe]

* A file already loaded is skipped, not loaded on top of itself.
* A file that a stopped run left half-written is loaded again from scratch.
* A table holding rows this kit did not load is left alone, unless you say otherwise.

```bash
EXAKIT_ON_EXISTING=replace exakit data-load ~/exports
```

`EXAKIT_ON_EXISTING` takes `skip` (the default), `replace` or `append`. Without a terminal the answer is `skip`. On a terminal you are asked.

## What you get at the end [#what-you-get-at-the-end]

Every file is listed with its table and the rows that landed, or the reason it did not load. A file the loader refuses leaves no empty table behind.

## From a notebook [#from-a-notebook]

```python
nb.exakit("data-load", "fraud_transactions")
own_data = nb.load_own_file("~/sales-data/orders.csv", "SALES", conn=connection)
```

See [Load data in the Data Scientist notebooks](/data-scientist/guides/load-data).

## An external source [#an-external-source]

Data in another database is not copied. It is connected with `exakit connect` and read where it lives. See [Sources](/data-scientist/concepts/sources).


# Run SQL (/kit/data/run-sql)



```bash
exakit sql 'SELECT COUNT(*) FROM AMAZON.ORDER_LINES'
```

It runs one statement and prints the result.

## Reads only unless you say otherwise [#reads-only-unless-you-say-otherwise]

A statement that would change data is refused unless you add `--write`.

```bash
exakit sql --write 'CREATE SCHEMA SCRATCH'
```

<Callout type="warn">
  `exakit sql` connects as the kit's admin user, and that user is not sandboxed. The read-only boundary is the MCP user that AI clients use, not this command.
</Callout>

## A saved statement [#a-saved-statement]

```bash
exakit sql --file ./report.sql
```

Comment lines and a trailing semicolon are dropped first. A statement can also come on standard input.

## Errors come with their fix [#errors-come-with-their-fix]

The three faults everyone hits first are turned into what to do:

| Fault                  | What you are told  |
| ---------------------- | ------------------ |
| Connection refused     | Run `exakit start` |
| `FETCH FIRST` or `TOP` | Use `LIMIT`        |
| Object not found       | Describe it first  |

The fix is printed first, with the error.

## For a script [#for-a-script]

```bash
exakit sql --json 'SELECT 1'
```

One JSON object comes back and nothing else: the rows and their count on success, or the error with a command to run, when there is one.

<Callout>
  On Windows PowerShell 5.1, a double quote inside an argument is dropped before `exakit` runs. Pass a statement with quoted names through `--file`.
</Callout>


# Semantic views (/kit/data/semantic-views)



The kit's semantic layer is **Exasol Semantic Views**, the database's own semantic layer. A model says what your data means in business terms: its entities (tables), the relationships between them, the dimensions you group by and the metrics you ask for. AI clients read it over MCP and answer from its metrics; notebooks ask it with Semantic SQL.

You do not write a model by hand. The kit builds it from what you approved:

| You approved                          | It becomes                                                      |
| ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A table's column map                  | An entity, with its key and grain                               |
| A link between two tables             | A relationship (many-to-one)                                    |
| A `time`, `category` or `flag` column | A dimension (a time column also gives `<column>_month`)         |
| A `measure` column                    | A fact, and the metrics `total_<column>` and `average_<column>` |
| Every table                           | A row count, `<table>_count`                                    |

A column marked **sensitive** is never a dimension and never a public fact.

## Installed when it is needed [#installed-when-it-is-needed]

Semantic Views is a marketplace add-on (`semantic-views`). The first approval installs it into the database, as this would:

```bash
exakit marketplace semantic-views
```

If that install fails, the approval still stands and says which command to run.

## One model per schema [#one-model-per-schema]

Approving a column map rebuilds its schema's model:

```bash
exakit describe AMAZON.ORDER_LINES --approve --role target=CANCELLED
```

The model is named after the schema (`amazon`) and its views are published in `SEM_<SCHEMA>` (`SEM_AMAZON.ORDER_LINES`). Approving a schema's links (`exakit describe --schema AMAZON --approve`) rebuilds it with the links as relationships.

## One model across sources [#one-model-across-sources]

A question often needs more than one schema: a sample dataset, your own files and one or more external sources. Build one model over all of them:

```bash
exakit describe --model sales_360 \
  --table AMAZON.ORDER_LINES --table MY_DATA.TARGETS --table VS_LOGISTICS.COURIER_DAILY \
  --link AMAZON.ORDER_LINES.SHIP_STATE=VS_LOGISTICS.STATE_LOGISTICS.STATE \
  --ai --dry-run
```

* Every table needs an approved column map first.
* `--link SCHEMA.TABLE.COLUMN=SCHEMA.TABLE.KEY` joins tables of different schemas. The key side must be unique. The approved links of each schema are used too.
* An external source (a virtual schema, `VS_<NAME>`) is read live: nothing is copied.
* `--dry-run` prints what would be built and writes nothing. Run it again without `--dry-run` to publish.

### Let the AI propose the fields [#let-the-ai-propose-the-fields]

With `--ai`, the model you set up for the kit (`EXAKIT_MODEL_ID` and `EXAKIT_PROVIDER_BASE_URL`) proposes business names, comments and synonyms for every field, and the metrics people will ask for: filtered totals (completed revenue), differences and ratios.

It is sent names, types, grains, column notes and a category's most frequent values. It is never sent a row, and never a sensitive column.

Every proposed metric is checked before it is used: it may only add up a fact of its view, combine that view's metrics, and filter on a dimension with one of its known values. The product validates it again when it is applied. A refused one is skipped, and the output names it and says why.

## Keep it current [#keep-it-current]

A model is built from what was approved at the time.

* Approving a column map rebuilds its schema's model and every multi-source model the table is in.
* After a new link or a new table, rebuild a model yourself:

```bash
exakit describe --model sales_360 --refresh
exakit describe --models                         # every model, and which the kit can refresh
```

The kit only rebuilds models it built. A model of the same name that someone else made is left alone.

## Ask a model [#ask-a-model]

A published view is queried with Semantic SQL: its metrics, grouped by its dimensions.

```sql
EXECUTE SCRIPT SEMANTIC_ADMIN.ENABLE_SEMANTIC_SQL();
SELECT ship_state, total_amount, orders_count
FROM SEM_SALES_360.ORDER_LINES
GROUP BY ship_state;
```

An AI client sets the preprocessor through the Exasol MCP server (`set_exasol_preprocessor`) and runs the same query. To see what a model holds, read `SEMANTIC_CATALOG.MODELS`, `ENTITIES`, `DIMENSIONS`, `METRICS` and `RELATIONSHIPS`.

## From a notebook [#from-a-notebook]

```python
semantic = nb.semantic_model(connection, "sales_360",
                             tables=["AMAZON.ORDER_LINES", "VS_LOGISTICS.COURIER_DAILY"],
                             links=["AMAZON.ORDER_LINES.SHIP_STATE=VS_LOGISTICS.STATE_LOGISTICS.STATE"],
                             preview=True)
semantic = semantic.publish()
nb.semantic_sql(connection, "SELECT ship_state, total_amount FROM SEM_SALES_360.ORDER_LINES GROUP BY ship_state")
nb.refresh_semantic(connection, "sales_360")
```

In the guided view, the **Semantic views** card in Understand does the same: pick the tables, let the AI propose the fields, preview, publish, refresh.


# All exakit commands (/kit/reference/commands)



{/* Generated by tools/nb_docs.py from setup/help/exakit.json. Edit those, then run the tool. */}

`exakit help <command>` prints a command's full reference on this computer, and `exakit catalog <word>`
searches them.

## Everyday [#everyday]

| Command            | Takes                                                                   | What it does                                                                    |
| ------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `exakit status`    | `[--json]`                                                              | Is the database up and healthy?                                                 |
| `exakit info`      | `[--json]`                                                              | Your connection details.                                                        |
| `exakit start`     | `[<service>]`                                                           | Start the database and every add-on service, or one of them.                    |
| `exakit stop`      | `[<service>]`                                                           | Stop the add-on services and the database, or one of them.                      |
| `exakit sql`       | `'<statement>' \| --file <path> \| (stdin) [--json] [--write] [--help]` | Run one SQL statement, with the error translated.                               |
| `exakit data-load` | `[<file-or-folder-or-dataset>] [--force]`                               | Load a dataset (downloaded only when you pick it), one file, or a whole folder. |
| `exakit logs`      | `[<target>] [-f] [--lines N] [--path] [--json]`                         | Every log the kit can show.                                                     |
| `exakit autostart` |                                                                         | Come back automatically after a restart?                                        |

## AI clients (MCP) [#ai-clients-mcp]

| Command             | Takes                      | What it does                       |
| ------------------- | -------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| `exakit mcp-setup`  |                            | Connect your AI clients.           |
| `exakit mcp-doctor` | `[clients] [--json]`       | Test and repair the AI connection. |
| `exakit mcp-status` | `[clients] [--json \| -j]` | Show managed MCP state per client. |

## External sources (virtual schemas) [#external-sources-virtual-schemas]

| Command          | Takes                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                | What it does                                                    |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `exakit connect` | `[source] [--name N] [--url STRING] [--set KEY=VALUE]... [--password-file F \| --password-stdin] [--storage-secret-file F] [--dry-run] [--yes] [--json]`                                                                                                                             | Query an external database from the local one (virtual schema). |
| `exakit source`  | `list\|issues [--status S]\|catalog\|show <name>\|describe <name> [TABLE] [--ddl] [--schema S]\|check <name>\|--all\|reauth <name> [--password-file F \| --password-stdin] [--storage-secret-file F]\|refresh <name>\|disconnect <name>\|remove <name> [--dry-run] [--yes] [--json]` | List, check and manage connected external sources.              |

## Personas and notebooks [#personas-and-notebooks]

| Command           | Takes                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `exakit persona`  | `list \| show <id> \| plan [<id>] [--json] \| add [<id>[,<id>]] \| remove <id>`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | Who the kit is set up for - Data Scientist or General: list, show, plan, add or remove one.                                                                                                       |
| `exakit notebook` | `[jupyterlab \| marimo] [check] [setup] [stop] [--no-browser] [--port <number>]`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        | Open JupyterLab or Marimo, connected to the local database (the notebook add-on).                                                                                                                 |
| `exakit describe` | `<SCHEMA.TABLE> [--sample <rows>] [--id <slug>] [--json] [--write <path>] \| <id\|SCHEMA.TABLE\|draft.yaml> --approve [--role <slot>=<COLUMN>]... [--owner <who>] [--no-comments] [--json] \| <id> --show [--version <n>] [--json] \| <id> --versions [--json] \| <id> --comments [--json] \| --schema <SCHEMA> [--approve [--link <TABLE.COLUMN>=<TABLE.KEY>]... [--unlink <TABLE.COLUMN>]... [--owner <who>] [--no-comments]] [--json] \| --model <NAME> --table <SCHEMA.TABLE>... [--link <SCHEMA.TABLE.COLUMN>=<SCHEMA.TABLE.KEY>]... [--ai] [--description <text>] [--dry-run] [--json] \| --model <NAME> --refresh [--json] \| --models [--json]` | Draft each column's role in a table (key, time, measure, category, flag, text, identifier, other), approve it, and publish it as an Exasol Semantic Views model for the notebooks and AI clients. |
| `exakit workflow` | `list \| show <id> [--json \| -j]`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      | The workflow logs the notebook helpers write: list them, show one.                                                                                                                                |

## Models and UDFs (udf-devkit, hidden for now) [#models-and-udfs-udf-devkit-hidden-for-now]

| Command            | Takes                                                                                                                                          | What it does                                                                                                                     |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `exakit mlflow`    | `start\|stop\|disable\|status\|url\|replay [action options]`                                                                                   | Start or stop the local MLflow server, show its address, or replay pending runs.                                                 |
| `exakit udf-setup` | `[--language python\|rust] [--force] [--yes] [--json]`                                                                                         | Python or Rust UDFs: install the official Python container (or the pinned Rust one) and prove it (the udf-devkit add-on).        |
| `exakit udf-use`   | `default [--language python\|rust] [--yes] [--json] \| <container.tar.gz> [--alias NAME] [--language python\|rust] [--yes] [--json] \| --list` | Install a script language container: the kit's prebuilt one for this database, or a tarball of your own.                         |
| `exakit udf-build` | `<requirements.txt> [--alias <NAME>] [--yes]`                                                                                                  | Build a container with your pinned packages and install it.                                                                      |
| `exakit udf-file`  | `<file> [<path in the bucket>]`                                                                                                                | Copy a file into BucketFS and print the path a UDF reads it from.                                                                |
| `exakit rust-udf`  | `new <name> [--coefficients <file>] \| build <name> \| deploy <name> [--schema <SCHEMA>] [--yes] [--json]`                                     | Create, build and deploy a Rust scoring UDF from exported coefficients.                                                          |
| `exakit model`     | `put\|inspect\|list\|rm\|prune\|template [arguments]`                                                                                          | Model files in the bucket directory: put one (digest recorded, /buckets path printed), list them, find the scoring UDF template. |

| Command              | Takes                                | What it does                                                             |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `exakit marketplace` | `[<addon-id>...] \| --list [--json]` | Optional add-ons: dashboards, notebooks, UDFs, dbt, scheduling and more. |

| `exakit uninstall`      | `[<addon-id>] [--dry-run] [--yes]`                                                                                                 | Remove what the kit installed.                        |
